identification.title: Agnus Dei
identification.notes: Written by Michael W. Smith alone; PraiseCharts gives the copyright as 1990 Milene Music, administered by Sony/ATV. The list's artist guess is right. It first appeared on Smith's 1990 pop-leaning album Go West Young Man and became a congregational standard after his 2001 live Worship recording. This is Smith's song, not the Latin liturgical Agnus Dei, though both take their title from John 1:29. A commenter on one review confuses it with Samuel Barber's unrelated piece of the same name; the credit to Smith is not in doubt. CCLI number not confirmed from a source read for this review.

claims.structuralNotes: A short, refrain-shaped song with a single repeated movement rather than separate verses. It is addressed directly to God and to the Lamb. It ascribes holiness and worth to God the Almighty and to the Lamb, echoing the heavenly worship of Revelation 4 and 5. It names the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb, calls for an alleluia, and declares the Lamb worthy. It does not narrate the cross, sin or the resurrection; it assumes them in the title and the Lamb imagery. No singular first person.

claims.claim: The Lord God Almighty is holy.

claims.claim: The Lamb is worthy of praise.
claims.subject: The worthiness of Christ

claims.claim: Christ is the Lamb, the sacrifice, given for sinners.
claims.subject: Christ as the sacrificial Lamb
claims.locationDetail: carried by the title and the Lamb language

strengths.title: The Lamb is named and worshipped
strengths.explanation: Christ is addressed under his sacrificial title and declared worthy, with no hedging about whom the praise is for. The Lamb imagery carries the atonement into the room even though the song does not narrate it.
strengths.scriptureRationale: Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world - the title the song is built on.

strengths.title: The throne-room worship of Revelation
strengths.explanation: The song takes the heavenly acclamation of the holy God and the worthy Lamb and puts it in the congregation's mouth. That is worship shaped by Scripture rather than by mood.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The Lamb who was slain is worthy to receive honour and glory - the acclamation the song borrows.

doctrinesAffirmed: The deity of Christ as the worshipped Lamb
theological.assessment: Nothing to correct. A brief, scriptural song of adoration that takes the Revelation acclamation to the Lamb and sings it. It states little of its own: the atonement is carried by the title rather than spelled out, and the cross, sin and resurrection are not narrated. That is a limit of scope, not an error. One lay review finds it consistent with Scripture.

strengths.title: Short and easy to hold
strengths.explanation: The text is brief and the movement repeats, so a room that has never heard it can join within a pass. It suits a time of quiet adoration or a response to the Word.

communal.vocalRangeNote: Published in several keys; no chart was read. Test the entry point with your own room, since the original recording suits a trained voice.

range.key: Not verified; published in multiple keys
range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: The same short confession of the Lamb's worth returns, which suits a text made of acclamation. The repetition does not substitute for content so much as dwell on a single scriptural claim.
communal.assessment: Congregational in words and form: brief, easy to learn, and addressed to God. It works as a response of adoration after the Word or at communion and does not depend on a lead vocal.

strengths.title: The Lamb and the Lord God Almighty are named
strengths.explanation: There is no vague addressee. The song names the holy God and the Lamb, and anyone who knows the Bible knows who is meant.

clarity.assessment: Clear to a churchgoer. One reviewer notes that an outsider might not recognise the Lamb as Jesus, which is fair: the song leans on the congregation's knowledge of John 1 and Revelation and does not explain itself.

synthesis.summary: A short song of adoration addressed to the holy Lord God Almighty and the worthy Lamb, taking the acclamation of Revelation 4 and 5 into the congregation's mouth. Christ is named by his sacrificial title. It states little beyond holiness and worth, and carries the atonement by implication rather than narration. No false claims.
